topic: The bridge that danced itself apart (1940)
claim: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted itself apart in the wind on Nov. 7, 1940, four months after opening, through aeroelastic flutter.

beats.caption: THE BRIDGE THAT DANCED
beats.vo: This bridge danced itself to pieces.

beats.caption: OPENED JULY 1940
beats.vo: In July 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened as the third longest suspension span in the world.

beats.caption: GALLOPING GERTIE
beats.vo: Its nickname was Galloping Gertie, because the deck bounced in the wind.

beats.caption: NOVEMBER 7, 1940
beats.vo: On November seventh, just four months later, the wind set the deck twisting, and every twist fed the next.

beats.caption: AEROELASTIC FLUTTER
beats.vo: Engineers call it aeroelastic flutter. The slim deck could not stop it, and it tore apart.

beats.caption: NOW BRIDGES DON'T DANCE
beats.vo: Since then, suspension bridges are stiffened and streamlined, so they can't dance.

sources.text: WSDOT, Tacoma Narrows Bridge history: https://www.wsdot.wa.gov/tnbhistory/ (opened July 1, 1940; third longest suspension span; collapsed Nov. 7, 1940)
WSDOT, Lessons from failure: https://wsdot.wa.gov/tnbhistory/bridges-failure.htm (torsional flutter; self-excited twisting; stiffened/streamlined designs since)

APS News, Nov. 7, 1940: Collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2016/11/collapse-of-tacoma-narrows-bridge (deck moved vertically in moderate wind; resonance explanation rejected)
Billah & Scanlan (1991), Am. J. Physics 59:118-124, 'Resonance, Tacoma Narrows Bridge failure, and undergraduate physics textbooks'
